topics.title: How plants work
topics.intro: Every part of a plant has a job. Roots drink and hold on, the stem carries water up like a pipe, leaves make food from sunlight, and flowers make seeds.
topics.teach: Explain how water gets from the soil to the leaves.
topics.talk: Put a white flower or a stick of celery in coloured water and watch it change colour over a day.

topics.title: Flowers, pollination and seeds
topics.intro: Flowers are a plant’s way of making seeds. Insects carry pollen from flower to flower, seeds form, and then the seeds travel to new places to grow.
topics.teach: Explain three ways seeds travel away from the parent plant.
topics.talk: Blow a dandelion clock together and count how far the seeds fly.

topics.title: Food and nutrition
topics.intro: Animals cannot make their own food like plants can. We need the right mix of foods: carbohydrates for energy, protein for growing, fruit and vegetables for vitamins, and a little fat.
topics.teach: Explain why a racing driver needs carbohydrates before a race.
topics.talk: Look at {her} dinner plate and sort the foods into groups together.

topics.title: Skeletons and muscles
topics.intro: Your skeleton holds you up, protects your insides and helps you move. Muscles pull on bones to make them move. Some animals have no bones at all!
topics.teach: Explain how muscles make your arm bend.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to feel the muscle at the front of {her} arm while bending and straightening it.

topics.title: Rocks and soils
topics.intro: There are three families of rock: igneous rocks made from cooled lava or magma, sedimentary rocks made from layers squashed together, and metamorphic rocks changed by heat and pressure.
topics.teach: Explain how a sedimentary rock forms.
topics.talk: Collect a few pebbles and test which ones soak up drops of water.

topics.title: Light, mirrors and shadows
topics.intro: We see things when light bounces off them into our eyes. Shiny surfaces reflect light well. Shadows change size when the light source moves.
topics.teach: Explain why your shadow gets bigger when you walk towards a torch.
topics.talk: Use a torch and a toy to make a shadow, then move the torch closer and further away.

topics.title: Forces, friction and magnets
topics.intro: Some forces need contact, like a push or friction. Magnets can push and pull without touching. Engineers think about friction all the time when they design racing cars.
topics.teach: Explain why racing tyres need lots of grip but a race car’s body needs to be smooth.
topics.talk: Roll a toy car down a ramp onto carpet, wood and a towel. Which surface stops it soonest?

topics.title: Thinking like a scientist
topics.intro: Scientists ask questions, make predictions and carry out fair tests. In a fair test you change only ONE thing and keep everything else the same.
topics.teach: Explain what makes a test fair.
topics.talk: Plan a test together: which paper aeroplane flies furthest? What must stay the same?

topics.title: Countries of Europe
topics.intro: Europe is the continent the UK belongs to. It has more than 40 countries, from icy Iceland in the north to sunny Greece in the south.
topics.teach: Name four countries in Europe and one fact about each.
topics.talk: When you see a car number plate or a football team from another country, find it on the map.

topics.title: UK cities, rivers and mountains
topics.intro: The UK has big cities, long rivers and high mountains. Ben Nevis in Scotland is the highest mountain in the whole UK.
topics.teach: Name the highest mountain in each of Scotland, Wales and England.
topics.talk: Find the nearest city and river to your home on the map.

topics.title: Volcanoes and earthquakes
topics.intro: The Earth’s outer layer, the crust, is cracked into giant pieces called plates. Where plates push, pull or slide past each other, we get earthquakes and volcanoes.
topics.teach: Explain why there are earthquakes in some places and not others.
topics.talk: Peel a satsuma and talk about how the Earth’s crust is broken into pieces like the peel.

topics.title: Compass points and grid references
topics.intro: The 8 points of the compass are north, north-east, east, south-east, south, south-west, west and north-west. Grid references help you find a square on a map: along the corridor, then up the stairs!
topics.teach: Explain how to find the square at grid reference C3.
topics.talk: Draw a treasure map of the garden with a grid, and give {him} a grid reference to find the treasure.

topics.title: Climate zones and biomes
topics.intro: Climate is the usual weather of a place over many years. Hot places near the Equator, cold places near the Poles, and in between, temperate places like the UK.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between weather and climate.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which biome {she} would like to explore, and what {she} would need to take.

topics.title: Solids, liquids and gases
topics.intro: Everything is a solid, a liquid or a gas. Heating and cooling can change one into another: ice melts into water, and water evaporates into water vapour.
topics.teach: Explain the journey of a raindrop round the water cycle.
topics.talk: Watch an ice cube melt on a plate, then talk about where puddles go on a sunny day.

topics.title: Teeth and digestion
topics.intro: Digestion breaks food into tiny pieces your body can use. It starts with your teeth and ends a long way later, after a journey through your stomach and intestines.
topics.teach: Explain the job of each type of tooth.
topics.talk: Look in a mirror together and find {her} incisors, canines and molars.

topics.title: Sorting living things with keys
topics.intro: Scientists sort living things into groups. A classification key asks yes-or-no questions, one at a time, until only one answer is left.
topics.teach: Explain how a key helps you name an animal you don’t know.
topics.talk: Make a yes/no key together for four toys or four family members.

topics.title: Circuits and switches
topics.intro: A circuit is a complete loop. Add more batteries and a bulb gets brighter; add more bulbs and each one gets dimmer. Conductors let electricity through; insulators don’t.
topics.teach: Explain why a bulb doesn’t light if there is a gap in the circuit.
topics.talk: Count the switches in your kitchen. What does each one complete?

items.prompt: Which part of a plant takes in water from the soil and holds it in place?
items.explain: Roots spread out underground to take in water and minerals, and anchor the plant.

items.prompt: Which part of a plant carries water up from the roots to the leaves?
items.explain: The stem works like a bundle of tiny drinking straws, and holds the plant up towards the light.

items.prompt: Which part of a plant makes food using sunlight?
items.explain: Leaves use sunlight, air and water to make the plant’s food. This is called photosynthesis.

items.prompt: What is the main job of a flower?
items.explain: Flowers attract insects so they can be pollinated and make seeds.

items.prompt: What does a plant need to grow well?

options.text: Light, water, air, warmth, room to grow and nutrients from the soil

options.feedback: Water alone isn’t enough: a plant in a dark cupboard goes pale and weak.
Most plants need light and warmth.

items.explain: Plants need light, water, air, warmth, space and nutrients.

items.prompt: A stick of celery stands in blue water. After a day, the leaves have blue streaks. What does this show?

options.text: Water travels up the stem to the leaves

options.feedback: The colour is a clue to where the water went.
They turned blue because coloured water travelled up.

items.explain: The coloured water travelled up tiny tubes in the stem all the way to the leaves.

items.prompt: Two bean plants are watered the same. One is kept in a dark cupboard. What will it look like after two weeks?

options.feedback: Without light, it can’t make food, so it loses its green colour.
Light makes a big difference.

items.explain: Without light the plant can’t make its food, so it grows pale and spindly.

items.prompt: What do plant roots take from the soil as well as water?
items.explain: Minerals in the soil keep the plant healthy. That is why gardeners add compost.

items.prompt: A tree trunk is a very big, woody…

options.feedback: The trunk is above ground, holding the tree up: a stem.
Leaves grow on the branches.

items.explain: A trunk does the same job as a stem: it holds the tree up and carries water.

items.prompt: What is it called when leaves make food using sunlight?
items.explain: Photo means light. Leaves use light to make sugar for the plant.

items.prompt: Put the life cycle of a flowering plant in order.
items: new seeds form and are spread
items.explain: Seed, sprouting, growing, pollination, seeds again: a cycle.

items.prompt: What powdery stuff do bees carry from flower to flower?
items.explain: Bees visit flowers for sweet nectar, and pollen sticks to their hairy bodies.

items.prompt: What is it called when pollen moves from one flower to another?
items.explain: After pollination, a flower can make seeds.

items.prompt: Why do many flowers have bright petals and a sweet smell?

options.text: To attract insects to pollinate them

options.feedback: Bright colours attract visitors.
Petals don’t keep the plant warm.

items.explain: Insects come for the nectar and carry pollen away with them.

items.prompt: Dandelion and sycamore seeds are spread by…
items.explain: Dandelion seeds have fluffy parachutes; sycamore seeds spin like helicopters.

items.prompt: Blackberry seeds are spread when birds eat the berries. How do the seeds get to a new place?
items.answer: they pass out in the bird’s droppings
items.explain: The seeds survive the bird’s tummy and land far away, with a little fertiliser!

items.prompt: Burdock seeds have tiny hooks. How are they spread?
items.explain: The hooks catch on fur (and socks!) and drop off somewhere new. They gave the idea for Velcro.

items.prompt: How are coconuts spread?
items.explain: Coconuts can float across the sea to grow on another beach.

items.prompt: Why is it good for seeds to travel away from the parent plant?

options.text: So the new plants don’t compete for light, water and space

options.feedback: Ha! It is about having enough to grow.

options.text: So the parent plant can rest
options.feedback: It is about giving the new plants room.

items.explain: If all the seeds fell in one spot, they would crowd each other out.

items.prompt: When a seed starts to sprout, it is called…
items.explain: A seed needs water and warmth to germinate. It doesn’t need light until the leaves appear.

items.prompt: Bread, pasta, rice and potatoes are mainly which food group?
items.explain: Carbohydrates give us energy. Racing drivers and athletes eat lots of them.

items.prompt: Meat, fish, eggs, beans and nuts are rich in which food group?
items.explain: Protein helps your body grow and repair muscles.

items.prompt: Why should we eat plenty of fruit and vegetables?

options.text: They give us vitamins, minerals and fibre to stay healthy
They are the only food with energy
options.feedback: Lots of foods have energy; fruit and veg give vitamins and fibre.
Not overnight!

items.explain: Vitamins and minerals keep your body working well; fibre helps digestion.

items.prompt: Butter, oil and cheese contain fat. How much fat should we eat?

options.text: A small amount: we need some, but not too much

options.feedback: Our bodies do need a little fat.
Too much fat is unhealthy.

items.explain: A balanced diet has a little fat, and only a little sugar.

items.prompt: How is the way humans get food different from plants?

options.text: Plants make their own food; humans have to eat food

options.feedback: Only plants can do that.
Plants make food; animals must eat.

items.explain: Animals, including humans, can’t make their own food, so we eat plants or other animals.

items.prompt: What should you drink most of to stay healthy?
items.explain: Our bodies are more than half water. Sugary drinks are bad for teeth.

items.prompt: Which is the most balanced lunch?

options.text: A chicken sandwich, an apple and water

options.feedback: Lots of fat and sugar, and no fruit or vegetables.

options.text: Just a big bowl of sweets
options.feedback: All sugar!

items.explain: Carbohydrate (bread), protein (chicken), fruit and water: balanced.

items.prompt: Turbo’s driver has a long race tomorrow. What should she eat tonight for slow-release energy?

options.text: A plate of pasta with vegetables

options.feedback: Sweets give a quick burst, then you feel tired.
You need fuel for a long race!

items.explain: Starchy carbohydrates like pasta release energy slowly over a long time.

items.prompt: Which of these is a job of your skeleton?
items.explain: Your skeleton supports you, protects organs (your skull protects your brain) and helps you move.

items.prompt: Which bone protects your brain?
items.explain: The skull is like a built-in crash helmet.

items.prompt: Which bones protect your heart and lungs?
items.explain: Your ribcage is like a cage around your heart and lungs.

items.prompt: What is the long chain of bones down the middle of your back called?
items.explain: The spine is made of 33 small bones called vertebrae.

items.prompt: Which is the longest bone in your body, in your thigh?
items.explain: The femur is also the strongest bone.

items.prompt: How do muscles move your bones?

options.text: They contract (get shorter) and pull on the bones
They push the bones from inside
options.feedback: Muscles can only pull, not push.
Muscles contract and relax.

items.explain: Muscles work in pairs: when one contracts and pulls, the other relaxes.

items.prompt: When you bend your arm, the muscle at the front (biceps) contracts. What does the muscle at the back do?

options.feedback: If both pulled at once, your arm wouldn’t move.
It relaxes and gets longer.

items.explain: Muscles work in pairs: one pulls while the other relaxes. To straighten your arm, they swap.

items.prompt: Where two bones meet, like at your knee or elbow, is called a…
items.explain: Joints let your skeleton bend.

items.prompt: An animal with a backbone is called a…

options.feedback: Invertebrates have NO backbone.
That is about what it eats.

items.explain: Fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals are vertebrates.

items.prompt: Which animal is an invertebrate (it has no backbone)?

options.feedback: Dogs have a backbone.
Frogs have a backbone.

items.explain: Worms, snails, insects, spiders and jellyfish have no backbone.

items.prompt: Beetles have a hard skeleton on the OUTSIDE of their bodies. What is it called?

options.feedback: Close! Its proper name is an exoskeleton.
Insects have no spine.

items.explain: Exo means outside. Crabs, beetles and ants have exoskeletons.

items.prompt: Rock that forms when hot melted rock (magma or lava) cools down is called…
items.explain: Igneous comes from the Latin word for fire. Granite and basalt are igneous.

items.prompt: Rock made from layers of sand, mud and shells squashed together over millions of years is called…
items.explain: Sandstone, limestone and chalk are sedimentary. Fossils are found in them.

items.prompt: Rock that has been changed by great heat and pressure underground is called…
items.explain: Metamorphic means changed shape. Marble was once limestone; slate was once mudstone.

items.prompt: In which type of rock are you most likely to find a fossil?

options.feedback: Igneous rock was once melted: any fossil would be destroyed.
Heat and pressure usually destroy fossils.

items.explain: Animals buried in mud and sand become fossils as the layers turn to sedimentary rock.

items.prompt: A rock that lets water soak into it is called…

options.feedback: Impermeable rocks let no water in.
That is about magnets.

items.explain: Chalk and sandstone are permeable. Granite and slate are impermeable.

items.prompt: Why is slate a good rock for roof tiles?

options.text: It is impermeable and splits into thin flat sheets

options.feedback: Crumbly rock would fall apart in the rain.
A roof must keep water OUT.

items.explain: Slate doesn’t let water through and splits into thin, flat pieces.

items.prompt: Put the steps of how a fossil forms in order.
items: it is buried by mud or sand
over millions of years the layers turn to rock
the rock wears away and the fossil is found
items.explain: Death, burial, rotting, rock forms, discovery.

items.prompt: Soil is made from tiny pieces of rock mixed with…
items.explain: Rotting leaves and dead creatures make soil rich, and worms mix it all up.

items.prompt: How could you test which of two rocks is harder?

options.text: Try scratching each one with a coin or a nail

options.feedback: Colour doesn’t tell you hardness.
Smell doesn’t show hardness.

items.explain: A harder rock scratches less. Keep the test fair: use the same object and the same push.

items.prompt: Which fossil hunter from Lyme Regis found the first complete ichthyosaur skeleton when she was a girl?
items.explain: Mary Anning was about 12 when her family found it, around 1811.

items.prompt: Granite is a hard, speckled rock. Which family of rock is it?
items.explain: Granite forms when magma cools slowly underground.

items.prompt: How do we see a book that is not a light source?

options.text: Light bounces off the book into our eyes
Our eyes send out light beams
options.feedback: Our eyes take light in; they don’t send it out.

options.text: The book glows in the dark
options.feedback: Books don’t make their own light.

items.explain: Light from a source (like the Sun or a lamp) reflects off objects and into our eyes.

items.prompt: When light bounces off a surface, it is called…
items.explain: Mirrors and shiny surfaces reflect light very well.

items.prompt: Which surface reflects light best?

options.feedback: Dark, rough surfaces reflect very little light.
Wood reflects some light, but a mirror reflects much more.

items.explain: Smooth, shiny surfaces reflect the most light.

items.prompt: Why do cyclists wear reflective strips at night?

options.text: Car headlights reflect off them, so drivers can see the cyclist

options.feedback: Reflective strips only shine when light hits them.
They are for being seen.

items.explain: Reflectors bounce car headlights straight back to the driver.

items.prompt: You hold a toy in front of a torch and move the torch CLOSER to the toy. What happens to the shadow?

options.feedback: Moving the light closer blocks more of the light, so the shadow grows.
There is still something blocking the light.

items.explain: The closer the light source, the bigger the shadow.

items.prompt: Which material makes the darkest shadow?

options.text: a transparent material, like clear glass
options.feedback: Light passes straight through clear glass.

options.text: a translucent material, like tissue paper
options.feedback: Tissue lets some light through, so its shadow is faint.

items.explain: Opaque materials block all light. Transparent ones let light through; translucent ones let some through.

items.prompt: A material you can see clearly through, like glass, is…
items.explain: Car windscreens must be transparent!

items.prompt: Why should you wear sunglasses on very bright days?

options.text: To protect your eyes from the Sun’s harmful light

options.feedback: Sunglasses make things darker.

options.text: To look like a racing driver
options.feedback: They might, but the real reason is protection.

items.explain: Sunlight contains invisible ultraviolet (UV) light that can damage eyes. Never look directly at the Sun.

items.prompt: Your shadow is shortest at about midday. Why?

options.text: The Sun is highest in the sky
The Sun is closest to the Earth at midday
options.feedback: It is about how HIGH the Sun is.
You are the same height all day!

items.explain: When the Sun is high, light comes from above and makes a short shadow.

items.prompt: Light travels in…

options.feedback: Light doesn’t bend round corners: that is why shadows form.
Light goes straight.

items.explain: Because light travels in straight lines, an object blocking it makes a shadow behind.

items.prompt: Which force does NOT need the objects to touch?

options.feedback: Friction needs two surfaces rubbing together.
A push needs contact.

items.explain: Magnetism (and gravity) act at a distance. Pushes, pulls and friction need contact.

items.prompt: Friction is a force that…

options.text: slows things down when surfaces rub together

options.feedback: That is not friction.
Friction happens everywhere surfaces touch.

items.explain: Rough surfaces make more friction; smooth surfaces make less.

items.prompt: Rosa rolls a toy car down a ramp onto three surfaces. On which will it travel furthest?

options.feedback: Carpet is rough: lots of friction.
Grass is bumpy and has lots of friction.

items.explain: The smoothest surface has the least friction, so the car rolls furthest.

items.prompt: To make the ramp test fair, what must stay the same each time?

options.text: the same car, the same ramp height and the same starting point

options.feedback: The surface is the ONE thing you change.
Then you couldn’t tell what made the difference.

items.explain: Change one thing (the surface); keep everything else the same.

items.prompt: Why do racing tyres need friction?

options.text: To grip the track so the car can speed up, brake and turn
To make the car slower on purpose
options.feedback: Grip helps the car go round corners fast.
It is about grip.

items.explain: Without friction the tyres would spin, and the car would slide off at the corners.

items.prompt: When is friction USEFUL?

options.text: When you brake on a bike
When you push a heavy box across the floor
options.feedback: Here friction makes it harder.

options.text: When a skier wants to go fast
options.feedback: Skiers wax their skis to REDUCE friction.

items.explain: Brakes work by friction. Without it, you couldn’t stop!

items.prompt: Which material is attracted to a magnet?
items.explain: Iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic. Most metals, like copper and aluminium, are not!

items.prompt: Are ALL metals magnetic?

options.text: No: only some, like iron, steel and nickel

options.feedback: Aluminium cans and copper pipes aren’t magnetic.
Iron and steel are.

items.explain: Recycling centres use big magnets to separate steel cans from aluminium ones.

items.prompt: You put the north pole of one magnet near the south pole of another. What happens?

options.feedback: Like poles repel; opposite poles attract.
Magnets always attract or repel each other.

items.explain: Opposite poles attract; like poles (N and N, or S and S) repel.

items.prompt: Why does a compass needle point north?

options.text: It is a tiny magnet, pulled by the Earth’s magnetism

options.feedback: Its lightness lets it turn, but magnetism points it.
It points north by itself.

items.explain: The Earth acts like a giant magnet. A compass needle lines up with it.

items.prompt: What force pulls things down towards the Earth?

options.feedback: Friction slows things down; it doesn’t pull them down.
Gravity pulls everything, not just magnetic things.

items.explain: Gravity pulls everything towards the Earth. It keeps the Moon going round us too.

items.prompt: What is a fair test?

options.text: A test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same

options.feedback: Fair here means the results can be trusted.

options.text: A test you do once quickly
options.feedback: Good scientists repeat tests.

items.explain: Changing one thing at a time shows what really caused the difference.

items.prompt: Before a test, Bleep says “I think the paper aeroplane with bigger wings will fly further.” What is this?

options.feedback: Results come AFTER the test.
A conclusion is what you decide after looking at results.

items.explain: A prediction is what you think will happen, and why.

items.prompt: Why should you repeat a test a few times?

options.text: To check the results are reliable, not a fluke
Because the first time is always wrong
options.feedback: It isn’t always wrong, but one result could be a fluke.
Repeating makes results more trustworthy.

items.explain: If the results are similar each time, you can trust them more.

items.prompt: Captain Nova is testing how far toy rockets fly. What is the best way to record it?

options.text: Measure the distance with a tape measure and write it in a table

options.feedback: Measuring is more accurate than guessing.
Write results down so you don’t forget.

items.explain: Scientists measure carefully and record results in tables and charts.

items.prompt: The results show that cars always roll further on wood than carpet. What is a good conclusion?

options.text: Smoother surfaces have less friction, so cars roll further

options.feedback: A conclusion should explain the pattern.

options.text: The car was tired on carpet
options.feedback: Cars don’t get tired!

items.explain: A conclusion explains what the results show, and why.

items.prompt: In a test of which plant food makes beans grow tallest, what should you MEASURE?

options.text: the height of each bean plant

options.feedback: Pot colour isn’t what you’re testing.
That doesn’t tell you about growth.

items.explain: You change the plant food, measure the height and keep everything else the same.
France is our nearest neighbour across the English Channel. The famous Le Mans 24-hour car race is held there.
Germany is in the middle of Europe. Karl Benz built the first petrol car there in 1885.
Spain is in the south-west of Europe, next to Portugal.
Italy is shaped like a boot. Rome, the city of the ancient Romans, is its capital.
Portugal is on the far western edge of Europe, beside the Atlantic Ocean.
Ireland is our neighbour across the Irish Sea. Its capital is Dublin.
The Netherlands is very flat. Lots of it is below sea level, protected by walls called dykes.
Belgium is a small country famous for chocolate and waffles.
Switzerland is a mountainous country with the high Alps.
Poland is in central Europe, east of Germany.
Norway has long, deep sea inlets called fjords. Vikings sailed from here.
Sweden is a long country in the north of Europe, with thousands of lakes.
Finland is in the far north. In midsummer the Sun barely sets!
Denmark is a small country made of a peninsula and many islands. LEGO was invented there.
Greece is in the south-east of Europe. The ancient Greeks held the first Olympic Games there.
Iceland is an island with volcanoes, geysers and glaciers.

items.prompt: What is the capital city of France?
items.explain: Paris is the capital of France.

items.prompt: What is the capital city of Germany?
items.explain: Berlin is the capital of Germany.

items.prompt: What is the capital city of Spain?
items.explain: Madrid is the capital of Spain.

items.prompt: What is the capital city of Italy?
items.explain: Rome is the capital of Italy.

items.prompt: What is the capital city of Ireland?
items.explain: Dublin is the capital of Ireland.

items.prompt: What is the capital city of Greece?
items.explain: Athens is the capital of Greece.

items.prompt: Which mountain range stretches across Switzerland, Austria, France and Italy?
items.explain: The Alps are the biggest mountain range entirely in Europe. Mont Blanc is its highest peak.

items.prompt: What links England and France under the sea?
items.explain: Trains travel through it under the English Channel. It opened in 1994.
Birmingham is the second biggest city in the UK, in the middle of England.
Manchester is a big city in the north-west of England.
Liverpool is a port city on the River Mersey, in the north-west of England.
Glasgow is the biggest city in Scotland.
Newcastle is in the north-east of England, on the River Tyne.
Bristol is in the south-west of England. Brunel’s Clifton Suspension Bridge is there.
York is an old city in the north of England. Vikings called it Jorvik.
Leeds is a big city in Yorkshire, in the north of England.
The Tay is the longest river in Scotland.
The Shannon is the longest river in Ireland (and in the British Isles).
The Wye flows along part of the border between England and Wales.
The Tweed flows along part of the border between England and Scotland.
The Great Ouse flows through the east of England to the sea at the Wash.
Ben Nevis, in Scotland, is the highest mountain in the UK: 1,345 metres.
Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon) is the highest mountain in Wales.
Scafell Pike, in the Lake District, is the highest mountain in England.
Slieve Donard is the highest mountain in Northern Ireland.

items.prompt: What is the highest mountain in the UK?
items.explain: Ben Nevis is 1,345 metres high, in the Scottish Highlands.

items.prompt: What is the longest river in the UK?
items.explain: The Severn starts in the mountains of Wales and flows into the Bristol Channel. The Thames is second.

items.prompt: What is the thin, rocky outer layer of the Earth called?
items.explain: The crust is broken into huge pieces called tectonic plates.

items.prompt: Put the layers of the Earth in order, from the outside to the middle.
items.explain: Like a peach: thin skin (crust), thick flesh (mantle), and a stone in the middle (core).

items.prompt: The Earth’s crust is cracked into giant pieces. What are they called?
items.explain: The plates move very slowly, about as fast as your fingernails grow.

items.prompt: What causes most earthquakes?

options.text: Tectonic plates suddenly slipping past each other

options.feedback: Lorries can shake the ground a little, but real earthquakes come from moving plates.
Storms are in the air, not underground.

items.explain: Plates get stuck, pressure builds up, then they slip suddenly and the ground shakes.

items.prompt: Where are most volcanoes found?

options.text: Along the edges of tectonic plates
In the middle of every country
options.feedback: They cluster where plates meet.
There are volcanoes all over the world, mostly at plate edges.

items.explain: The “Ring of Fire” around the Pacific Ocean has hundreds of volcanoes.

items.prompt: The ring of volcanoes and earthquakes around the Pacific Ocean is called the…
items.explain: It stretches past Japan, New Zealand, the west coast of America and Chile.

items.prompt: Which active volcano is on the island of Sicily, in Italy?
items.explain: Etna is one of the most active volcanoes in the world.

items.prompt: A volcano that has not erupted for thousands of years but might again is…

options.feedback: Active volcanoes erupt often, or have erupted recently.
Extinct volcanoes are not expected to erupt ever again.

items.explain: Active: erupts often. Dormant: sleeping. Extinct: finished for good. Edinburgh Castle stands on an extinct volcano!

items.prompt: What should you do during an earthquake if you are indoors?

options.text: Drop, cover under a strong table, and hold on

options.feedback: Glass and falling things are dangerous. Stay under cover.

options.text: Stand in the middle of the room
options.feedback: Get under something strong.

items.explain: “Drop, cover and hold on” protects you from falling objects.

items.prompt: Which European island country has many volcanoes and uses their heat to warm homes?
items.explain: Iceland sits on the edge of two plates. Hot water from underground heats houses.

items.prompt: What direction is halfway between north and east?

options.feedback: South-east is between south and east.
North-west is between north and west.

items.explain: The 8 points: N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW.

items.prompt: What direction is opposite north-east?

options.feedback: Opposite north is south, and opposite east is west: south-west.
Turn right round: north-east → south-west.

items.explain: Opposite N is S; opposite E is W. So opposite NE is SW.

items.prompt: Put these directions in order, going clockwise from north.
items.explain: Clockwise: N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW.

items.prompt: On a map grid with letters along the bottom and numbers up the side, how do you read grid reference C4?

options.text: Go along to column C, then up to row 4
Go up to 4, then along to C, in any order
options.feedback: Always go along first: “along the corridor, then up the stairs”.
Rows are usually counted up from the bottom.

items.explain: Along the corridor (letters), then up the stairs (numbers).

items.prompt: Bleep the droid faces north and turns 90° clockwise. Then it turns 45° more clockwise. Which way is Bleep facing?

options.feedback: That is after the first turn. 45° more goes to south-east.
North-east is only 45° from north.

items.explain: North → east is 90°. Another 45° clockwise reaches south-east.

items.prompt: In the UK, the Sun rises roughly in the…

options.feedback: The Sun SETS in the west.
In the UK, the Sun is never in the north at midday.

items.explain: The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west.

items.prompt: What does the key on a map tell you?

options.text: What the symbols on the map mean

options.feedback: It is a different kind of key!
That is the compass or north arrow.

items.explain: A key (or legend) explains the symbols: a blue line is a river, a cross might be a church.

items.prompt: On a map, 1 cm stands for 1 km. Two towns are 5 cm apart on the map. How far apart are they really?

options.feedback: That is the distance on paper. Each centimetre stands for a kilometre.
Each cm is 1 km, so 5 cm is 5 km.

items.explain: The scale tells you how map distances match real distances.

items.prompt: What is the difference between weather and climate?

options.text: Weather is day to day; climate is the usual weather over many years

options.feedback: Weather changes daily. Climate is the long-term pattern.

options.text: Climate only happens in hot countries
options.feedback: Every place has a climate.

items.explain: Today’s rain is weather. “The UK is mild and wet” is climate.

items.prompt: The UK has mild summers and cool, wet winters. What kind of climate is this?
items.explain: Temperate climates are not too hot and not too cold.

items.prompt: Hot, wet places near the Equator have which climate?
items.explain: Rainforests grow in tropical climates.

items.prompt: The very cold climates near the North and South Poles are called…
items.explain: Polar regions have long, dark winters and freezing temperatures.

items.prompt: A large area with its own climate, plants and animals, like a desert or a rainforest, is called a…

options.feedback: A continent is a big area of land; it can contain many biomes.
Biomes cross country borders.

items.explain: Biomes include rainforest, desert, grassland, tundra and ocean.

items.prompt: Lions, zebras and giraffes live on hot grasslands in Africa. What is this biome called?

options.feedback: Tundra is cold and treeless, near the Arctic.
Rainforests are thick forests, not open grasslands.

items.explain: Savannas are hot grasslands with a wet season and a dry season.

items.prompt: Which biome is cold, treeless and has frozen ground for most of the year?

options.feedback: Hot deserts are dry, but not frozen.
Rainforests are hot and wet.

items.explain: The tundra is near the Arctic. Reindeer and Arctic foxes live there.

items.prompt: Antarctica gets very little rain or snow. Which word describes it?

options.feedback: It is far too cold and dry.
It is covered in ice.

items.explain: A desert is any place with very little rain. Antarctica is the biggest desert on Earth!

items.prompt: Which of these is a solid?

options.feedback: Juice is a liquid: it flows.
Steam is a gas.

items.explain: Solids keep their shape. Liquids flow. Gases spread out to fill any space.

items.prompt: What is special about a liquid?

options.text: It flows and takes the shape of its container

options.feedback: That is a solid.

options.text: It spreads out to fill a whole room
options.feedback: That is a gas.

items.explain: Pour water into a jug, then a bowl: it takes each shape.

items.prompt: When a solid turns into a liquid, like ice turning into water, it is called…
items.explain: Heating makes solids melt. Chocolate melts in your hand!

items.prompt: What temperature does water freeze at?
items.explain: Water freezes into ice at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.

items.prompt: When water turns into water vapour (a gas), it is called…
items.explain: Puddles disappear on sunny days because the water evaporates.

items.prompt: When water vapour cools and turns back into liquid water, like on a cold window, it is called…
items.explain: The droplets on the bathroom mirror after a bath are condensation.

items.prompt: Put the water cycle in order, starting with the sea.
items: rivers carry water back to the sea
items.explain: Evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection: round and round.

items.prompt: Which of these is a gas?

options.feedback: Milk is a liquid.
Each grain of sand is a solid.

items.explain: Air is a mixture of gases. You can’t see it, but you can feel wind.

items.prompt: Which teeth at the front of your mouth are for biting and cutting?
items.explain: Incisors are flat and sharp, like little chisels.

items.prompt: Which pointed teeth are for tearing food?
items.explain: Canine means dog-like. Meat-eaters like wolves have big canines.

items.prompt: Which big, flat teeth at the back are for grinding and chewing?
items.explain: Molars crush food. Plant-eaters like cows have lots of big molars.

items.prompt: Put the journey of food through the body in order.
items.explain: Mouth, food pipe, stomach, small intestine (nutrients absorbed), large intestine (water absorbed).

items.prompt: What happens to food in the stomach?

options.text: It is churned up and mixed with acid to break it down

options.feedback: Food is broken down step by step first.
The stomach is busy churning and mixing.

items.explain: Stomach acid and churning muscles turn food into a soupy mush.

items.prompt: Where do most nutrients pass from food into the blood?

options.feedback: Digestion starts in the mouth, but nutrients are absorbed later.
Teeth break food up.

items.explain: The small intestine is about 6 metres long, with a huge surface for absorbing nutrients.

items.prompt: Why should you brush your teeth twice a day?

options.text: To remove plaque, which can cause tooth decay

options.feedback: Brushing keeps them healthy, not bigger.

options.text: To make them whiter than snow
options.feedback: The main reason is stopping decay.

items.explain: Bacteria in plaque turn sugar into acid that rots teeth.

items.prompt: What liquid in your mouth starts to break food down and makes it easier to swallow?
items.explain: Saliva (spit) softens food and starts digesting starch.

items.prompt: What is a classification key?

options.text: A set of yes/no questions that helps you name or group a living thing
A key that opens a zoo
options.feedback: It is a different kind of key!

options.text: A list of animals in alphabetical order
options.feedback: A key uses questions, not the alphabet.

items.explain: Each question splits the group in two until only one answer is left.

items.prompt: A key asks: “Does it have 6 legs?” Which animal goes down the YES branch?

options.feedback: Spiders have 8 legs.
Snails have no legs.

items.explain: Insects have 6 legs. Ladybirds are insects.

items.prompt: Which is a good question for a key?

options.feedback: People would disagree! Key questions need clear yes/no answers.
That depends on who answers.

items.explain: Good key questions are about features everyone can check.

items.prompt: You want to separate a fish, a bird, a dog and a snake. Which first question splits them into two groups of two?

options.feedback: All four have backbones, so that doesn’t split them.
They are all alive.

items.explain: Legs: bird and dog. No legs: fish and snake. Then ask another question for each pair.

items.prompt: A key asks: “Does it have a backbone?” Which goes down the NO branch?

options.feedback: Sharks are fish, with a backbone (made of cartilage).
Penguins are birds: they have a backbone.

items.explain: Jellyfish are invertebrates.

items.prompt: Plants can be sorted into flowering plants and non-flowering plants. Which is a non-flowering plant?

options.feedback: Daisies flower.
Apple trees have blossom.

items.explain: Ferns and mosses make spores instead of seeds.

items.prompt: What happens if you add a second battery to a circuit with one bulb?

options.feedback: More batteries push more electricity: brighter.
The extra battery makes a difference.

items.explain: More batteries (cells) make a bulb brighter, or a motor faster.

items.prompt: What happens if you add a second bulb in a loop with one battery?

options.feedback: They share the battery’s push, so each is dimmer.
Both light, but dimly.

items.explain: The bulbs share the electricity from the battery.

items.prompt: Why are electric wires covered in plastic?

options.text: Plastic is an insulator, so it stops electricity escaping and keeps us safe

options.feedback: The colours help electricians, but plastic is for safety.
Plastic does NOT conduct electricity.

items.explain: Copper inside conducts electricity; plastic outside insulates.

items.prompt: You put a spoon in the gap of a circuit and the bulb lights. What does that tell you?

options.text: The spoon is a conductor (probably metal)

options.feedback: Insulators would leave the bulb off.
It lit, so it works!

items.explain: Testing materials in a circuit gap shows conductors and insulators.

items.prompt: In a circuit, what does a cell (battery) provide?
items.answer: the push that makes electricity flow
items.explain: The cell pushes electricity round the circuit.

items.prompt: Turbo’s team builds a toy car with a motor and a battery. How could they make it go faster?

options.text: Add another bulb in the circuit
options.feedback: That would share the electricity and slow the motor.
Red is fast-looking, but it doesn’t change the circuit!

items.explain: More cells give the motor more push.
